approachQuestion.prompt: Clean a nested integer value by removing every zero integer, then removing every list that becomes empty. Preserve the order and nesting of all surviving entries. Return NONE if the entire root disappears; otherwise return a fresh cleaned value. Examples: [0,[0,2],[],[0]] returns [[2]]; [0,[]] returns NONE; 5 returns 5 as a fresh record.
constraints: A value is either a signed 32-bit integer or an ordered list of values; lists may be empty.
The input is finite, acyclic, and has no shared subobjects. There are n total integer and list objects, including the root, with 1 ≤ n ≤ 100000; maximum nesting depth is h ≤ 1000.
Do not modify the input. Indexing a list, reading a tag, and integer comparisons take constant time.
NONE is distinct from an empty list. Copied output records are fresh; do not reuse input records. Allocation and amortized child append take constant time.

options.text: Remove only lists that were empty in the original input, after deleting zeros.
options.feedback: [0] becomes empty during cleaning and must disappear too.

options.text: Promote every surviving grandchild directly into its grandparent, deleting all list boundaries.
Return NONE for a zero leaf and a fresh copy for any other leaf. For each list, clean its children once, retain only non-NONE results, and return NONE if none survived.
options.feedback: A parent decides emptiness only after learning which transformed children remain.

options.text: Deep-copy everything, then repeatedly scan and delete zero leaves and empty lists until a full scan changes nothing.
options.feedback: It reaches the correct fixed point, but can repeatedly revisit ancestors instead of finishing each child before its parent.

feedback.reason: Clean children before deciding whether their parent list survives.
details: Clean in postorder. A zero leaf returns NONE; a nonzero leaf returns a fresh record. At a list, create an empty result list, clean children one by one, and append each surviving returned value. If the result list is still empty return NONE, otherwise return that list. Empty discarded lists are immediately released.

Clean children before deciding whether their parent list survives. Removing a zero may make its containing list empty, which can empty an ancestor too. An absent result is different from retaining an empty list.
“Remove only lists that were empty in the original input, after deleting zeros.”: [0] becomes empty during cleaning and must disappear too.
“Promote every surviving grandchild directly into its grandparent, deleting all list boundaries.”: [0,[0,2]] must become [[2]], not [2].

“Return NONE for a zero leaf and a fresh copy for any other leaf. For each list, clean its children once, retain only non-NONE results, and return NONE if none survived.”: A parent decides emptiness only after learning which transformed children remain.

“Deep-copy everything, then repeatedly scan and delete zero leaves and empty lists until a full scan changes nothing.”: It reaches the correct fixed point, but can repeatedly revisit ancestors instead of finishing each child before its parent.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze method-1 as described in the revealed method. Let n and h have the meanings in Q1. Use child indices and references without copying lists. Count active call frames; exclude input and returned output. There is no tail-call elimination. No hashing is used. Allocation and append are constant amortized cost. Surviving records belong to the output; count temporary discarded empty-list records and call frames, and release discarded records immediately. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair among the options.

feedback.reason: Postorder cleanup visits every record and keeps only depth-bounded temporary state.
details: All objects are visited once. A nonempty constructed list survives into the output, while discarded lists are empty. Thus auxiliary live records outside the output are bounded by the pending nesting path.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Nested calls remain active along a path; their storage must be counted.
“O(n²) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: Each object is processed once without rescanning or copying its descendants.
“O(h + 1) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: A shallow but wide input can still require inspecting every object.
